title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 50
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Faster Than the Messenger
passages.text:
A. Until the telegraph, information travelled at the speed of a person carrying it, and every institution was built around that fact. Prices in two cities could differ for as long as it took a rider to cover the distance between them, military orders described a situation that had already changed, and the news a newspaper printed was a report of what had been true some days earlier. The telegraph broke the connection between the movement of a message and the movement of a body, and almost nothing that depended on it stayed the same.

B. The change in commerce came first and was the most immediate. Merchants had made their living partly from knowing prices that others did not, and when quotations from distant markets arrived within minutes that advantage evaporated; markets in different places converged into single markets with one price, and trading shifted from exploiting differences to anticipating movements. A profession disappeared and another took its place.

C. Building the network required solving problems that had no precedent. Signals weaken over distance and had to be received and retransmitted; submarine cables had to survive laying, pressure and corrosion, and several early attempts failed expensively before the engineering was understood. The undersea links in particular consumed fortunes and took years, and the first successful ones worked slowly and briefly before failing.

D. The economics pushed towards concentration from the beginning. A network is more valuable the more places it reaches, so operators competed to acquire one another rather than to serve the same routes, and the result in most countries was a single dominant private company or a state monopoly. This pattern — networks tending towards one operator — was observed here before it was observed anywhere else.

E. The social effects were exaggerated at the time in terms that are now familiar. Commentators predicted that instant communication between nations would make war obsolete by removing misunderstanding, that it would unify humanity, and that distance would cease to matter. None of this happened, the same predictions were made about every subsequent communication technology, and the persistence of the pattern is more interesting than any individual instance of it.

F. What did change was the structure of organisations. A company could now manage operations it could not see, so head offices grew, standardised reporting appeared, and decisions moved away from the people present at the place a decision concerned. The large centralised firm is a creature of cheap fast communication, and its shape was determined by what could be transmitted rather than by any theory of management.

passages.title: The Structure That Made Flight Possible
passages.text:
A feather is a more remarkable object than the flight it enables. It is made of a single protein, grows from a follicle in the skin as a hair does, and assembles itself into a branched structure whose parts hook together — barbs off a central shaft, barbules off the barbs, and microscopic hooks that link adjacent barbules into a continuous surface that can be pulled apart and reconnected by preening. The result is light, stiff in one direction, flexible in another, and repairable.

Feathers did not evolve for flight, which is now established well enough to be uncontroversial. Simple filamentous feathers appear on animals that could not fly and were not close to flying, and the branched, asymmetric feathers required for a flight surface appear considerably later. Whatever the first ones were for — insulation, display, and protection are the candidates — flight was a later use of a structure that already existed.

Insulation is the likeliest original function and the argument for it is straightforward. A covering of fine filaments traps air and reduces heat loss, which is useful to any animal maintaining a body temperature above its surroundings, and the fossil evidence places filamentous coverings on animals whose size and inferred metabolism make heat retention plausible. Display is also credible and is harder to test, since colour rarely survives, though microscopic structures that produce colour sometimes do.

The flight feather is a specialised form and its asymmetry is the diagnostic feature. A feather with the shaft displaced towards the leading edge twists in a controlled way under airflow, which allows air to pass on the upstroke and be pushed on the downstroke, and symmetric feathers do not behave this way. Finding asymmetric feathers in the fossil record is therefore evidence about flight in a way that finding feathers is not.

Maintenance is a large part of what a bird's day contains and it is easy to overlook. Feathers wear, and because they are dead structures they cannot repair themselves, so they must be cleaned, oiled, reconnected by preening and eventually replaced entirely — a moult that costs energy and, in most species, is spread so that flight is never lost. Birds that moult all their flight feathers at once are flightless for the period and are almost all species that can afford to be.

The engineering interest is in properties that manufactured materials achieve individually and not together. A feather is stiff enough to transmit force, flexible enough not to break, light for its strength, self-organising in manufacture, and repairable by an operation as simple as drawing it through a beak. Materials science has produced better performance on any single one of these and nothing that combines them, which is the usual finding when a biological structure is examined closely.

passages.title: Money Sent Home
passages.text:
Money sent home by people working abroad exceeds development aid to the countries receiving it by a wide margin, and it behaves quite differently from aid in ways that make the comparison worth drawing carefully. It arrives directly to households rather than through governments, it is spent according to the recipients' own priorities, and it is remarkably stable — rising when the home economy weakens, because the reason for sending it is need rather than opportunity.

What the money is spent on has been the subject of a long and somewhat misdirected argument. Critics have observed that most of it goes on food, housing, healthcare and school fees rather than on business investment, and have described this as consumption rather than development. The observation is correct and the conclusion does not follow: school fees paid are education purchased, and a household that eats adequately and receives treatment is a household whose members can work. The distinction between consumption and investment is doing less work here than it appears to.

The cost of sending it is where the clearest failure sits. Transfer fees have historically absorbed a substantial share of small remittances, and the burden falls most heavily on the smallest transfers to the poorest destinations, where the corridors are thin and the competition weak. Reducing this cost transfers money to poor households at no expense to anyone except the intermediaries, which makes it one of the few genuinely uncontested propositions in development policy.

The effects on the country of origin are not uniformly positive and the awkward parts are usually omitted. Large inflows can raise the exchange rate and make other exports less competitive; the departure of trained people removes capacity that was expensive to create, particularly in health systems; and households receiving transfers sometimes reduce their own labour, which is rational for them and reduces measured output. These effects are real, they vary enormously by country, and they do not add up to an argument against migration.

The counterpart effects in destination countries are studied more and reported less faithfully. The evidence on wages is that effects on native workers are small and concentrated among earlier migrants with similar skills; the evidence on public finances depends almost entirely on the age structure of who arrives, since working-age arrivals pay in for years before drawing out. These are empirical questions with reasonably well-established answers that bear little resemblance to how they are usually discussed.

What would improve outcomes most has little to do with the arguments that dominate. Cheaper transfers, portable pension and social security entitlements, recognition of qualifications across borders, and safe legal routes that remove the need to pay smugglers would each produce measurable gains for migrants and for both countries. None of them requires anyone to change their mind about immigration in general, which may be why they receive so little attention.
